entities.summary:
Cologne Cathedral (Kölner Dom) is Germany's most visited landmark and the largest Gothic church in Northern Europe, taking 632 years to complete — construction began in 1248 CE and finished in 1880, making it the world's longest-running building project. A UNESCO World Heritage site housing the Shrine of the Three Kings (purportedly containing relics of the Biblical Magi), it was medieval Germany's greatest pilgrimage destination.

The cathedral was begun under Archbishop Konrad von Hochstaden to house the Shrine of the Three Kings, brought from Milan in 1164 by Emperor Frederick Barbarossa. Construction proceeded enthusiastically through the 14th century, reaching the choir (1322) and the south tower base (1437), then stalled for 400 years when medieval funding dried up and cranes stood idle against the unfinished towers. The cathedral's completion in the 1840s-1880s, financed by the Prussian state and enthusiastic German nationalism, was a deliberate symbol of German national unity during the period leading to unification in 1871.

The cathedral survived WWII with remarkable success — fourteen Allied bombing raids damaged but did not destroy it, and its undamaged spires became a navigation landmark for Allied pilots over the devastated city. The building contains masterpieces including the Gero Cross (c. 970 CE), the oldest surviving monumental crucifix north of the Alps; the Altar of the City Patrons (c. 1440); and the Shrine of the Three Kings in gold and enamel.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Cologne Cathedral's 632-year construction history made it both a masterpiece of Gothic engineering and a symbol of German national identity, surviving World War II as a beacon amid devastation.
